analysis.one_liner: Caps the cost of protecting endangered species on public construction projects at 10% of project costs.
analysis.headline: The bill to exempt public construction projects from paying more than 10% of their costs for endangered species protection died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Endangered Species Act so that any public construction project — federal, state, or local — could never be required to spend more than 10% of its total budget on mitigating harm to endangered or threatened species and their habitat. If protecting a species around a dam, highway, or building project would cost more than that cap, the project could simply skip it. The bill never moved past the House committee it was referred to and received no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If the bill had passed, construction firms and public agencies carrying out federally funded or federally permitted building projects would have saved money, because the government could no longer require them to fund habitat protection measures costing more than a tenth of the project budget. The Endangered Species Committee could likewise have been barred from imposing any mitigation exceeding the cap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps total required mitigation costs at 10% of project costs for any federal agency construction project, and for federal permits authorizing state or local construction projects.
It would have barred the Secretary of the Interior or Commerce from imposing any measures to minimize impacts on endangered species if those measures' aggregate cost exceeded the 10% cap.
It would have prohibited the Endangered Species Committee — the cabinet-level panel that can exempt projects from the Act — from establishing mitigation exceeding 10% of project costs.
It would also have applied the cap to incidental take permits, meaning public projects could avoid measures to minimize harm to endangered species when those measures exceeded 10% of costs.

analysis.who_pays: Endangered and threatened species and the habitat they depend on would have borne the cost: projects that would have been required to fund habitat protection could walk away once costs crossed the cap. The public also loses the environmental benefits of intact habitat, and any mitigation burden that did remain would fall more heavily on smaller projects where 10% is a larger share.

drawbacks.text: Supporters argued the cap would give cost certainty to public construction projects, but critics of such caps note that a fixed percentage limit does not scale with the actual biological need: a costly habitat measure on a very large project could be abandoned even when it was essential to the species' survival.

The bill removes the flexibility of the existing consultation process, under which agencies work case-by-case with wildlife scientists to design mitigation; a flat 10% rule could force abandonment of effective protection on big projects and waste on trivial ones.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to construction budgets come directly at the expense of species protection: the bill converts a science-based, case-by-case mitigation process into a rigid dollar cap, so the larger the project, the more habitat protection it could decline to pay for. The benefit is lower, more predictable costs for public works; the cost is weaker legal protection for endangered wildlife, concentrated on exactly the biggest projects.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Resources Committee two days after it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Calvert introduced the bill in the House on May 12, 1999, with one Republican cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Resources the same day and was referred to the Department of the Interior for comments on May 20, 1999.
No further action was taken: the Resources Committee never reported the bill, and it received no floor vote before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Endangered and threatened species and their habitat are better off, because the existing Endangered Species Act mitigation requirements remained in force. Construction and public works interests lost the cost cap they were seeking.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Republicans, and no Democrat supported the bill; opposition never became a recorded vote because the bill died in committee.

industries.note: The bill would have relieved public construction projects and federally permitted state and local projects of any mitigation costs above 10% of the project budget, cutting compliance costs. Its death left the Endangered Species Act's mitigation requirements intact, and the cost savings the industry sought never materialized.

Mitigation requirements under the Endangered Species Act generate demand for habitat restoration and biological assessment work on public projects. By capping mitigation spending, the bill would have shrunk that demand — an outcome whose main effect on the public would have been weaker habitat protection.
